title: The Man of Al-Yaman and His Six Scholars
summary: A wealthy and enlightened nobleman of Yemen had educated his six daughters in six distinct arts of the mind: the first in Astronomy, the second in Medicine, the third in Jurispr...
keywords: the man of al-yaman and his six slave-girls
full_text:
A wealthy and enlightened nobleman of Yemen had educated his six daughters in six distinct arts of the mind: the first in Astronomy, the second in Medicine, the third in Jurisprudence, the fourth in Poetry and Music, the fifth in Mathematics and Architecture, and the sixth in Philosophy and Ethics.

When business brought them to Baghdad, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid heard of this extraordinary assembly of intellect and summoned the family to his palace.

The Caliph challenged them to a friendly contest of wisdom: each scholar was to present an argument proving that her discipline was the foundation of human happiness and good governance.

The Astronomer spoke of the celestial spheres, the navigation of ships across trackless seas, and the majesty of the starry heavens. The Physician spoke of the preservation of life, the harmony of bodily humors, and the sacred relief of pain. The Jurist demonstrated how justice, fair laws, and the defense of the weak preserve peace in the commonwealth.

The Poet sang of how music and verse soften the human heart, inspiring empathy and courage. The Mathematician demonstrated how geometry builds bridges, aqueducts, and domes that endure through centuries. Finally, the Philosopher showed that without virtue, truth, and ethical conscience, all sciences become hollow instruments of vanity.

Harun al-Rashid listened with enraptured delight, applauding each discourse. He declared: 'None has surpassed the other, for wisdom is a single magnificent garden, and each of you tends a necessary blossom! No realm can stand on steel alone; it flourishes on science, art, and justice.' The Caliph bestowed royal gifts upon each of the six scholars and established a grand academy in Baghdad to teach their disciplines.
moral: Diverse branches of learning—science, art, and virtue—enrich human civilization like jewels in a single crown.
